## Short version

A TLB (translation lookaside buffer) is a small CPU cache of recent address translations. On a big-memory server, each miss can cost several slow memory reads. Huge pages reduce the misses, with new risks for memory use and latency.

## Words used here

- **Page**: a fixed-size block of memory. The default size on x86-64 is 4 KiB.
- **Page table**: the tree in memory that maps virtual pages to physical pages.
- **Page walk**: the CPU reads the page table after a TLB miss.
- **Leaf tables**: the last level of the page table.
- **THP (Transparent Huge Pages)**: the Linux feature that creates huge pages automatically.
- **hugetlbfs**: the Linux interface to a reserved set of huge pages.
- **NUMA (non-uniform memory access)**: each CPU socket has its own local memory.
- **DRAM**: main memory, outside the CPU caches.

## 1. What a TLB is

- Programs use virtual addresses. The CPU translates each one to a physical address.
- The page table holds the mapping. On x86-64 it is a tree with 4 levels [Ref1].
- The TLB stores recent translations. A hit needs no extra memory read.
- A miss starts a page walk. The walk reads one table entry per level.
- A core has a small first-level TLB and a larger second-level TLB.

```
virtual address -> [ TLB ] --hit--> physical address (0 extra reads)
                      |
                     miss
                      v
              page walk through the page table:
  4 KiB page:  L4 -> L3 -> L2 -> L1   = 4 memory reads
  2 MiB page:  L4 -> L3 -> L2         = 3 memory reads
  1 GiB page:  L4 -> L3               = 2 memory reads
```

- L4 to L1 are the page table levels, from root to leaf.
- Newer servers can use 5 levels. Then each walk has one more read.
- The diagram is simplified. The CPU also caches the upper levels [Ref1]. So many real walks need fewer reads.

## 2. Why misses are expensive on a big-memory server

The second-level TLB of a recent Intel server core has about 2048 entries (est.).

- **Small coverage.** 2048 entries × 4 KiB cover 8 MiB. A 512 GiB data set is 65,536 times larger.
- **Large page tables.** 1 TiB of mapped memory needs 2 GiB of leaf tables. That exceeds the CPU cache. So the last read of a walk often comes from DRAM.
- **Slow reads.** One DRAM read takes about 100 ns (est., about 300 cycles at 3 GHz). A TLB hit needs none.
- **Random access.** A hash table or a graph traversal accesses pages in random order. Then almost every access can miss.
- **NUMA.** The page table can be in the memory of another socket. Then each walk read takes longer.
- **Virtual machines.** A miss can need up to 24 memory reads. Each guest table read needs its own host translation [Ref2].
- **Measured cost.** One study measured big-memory server workloads. They spent up to 10% of execution cycles on TLB misses, even with huge pages [Ref3].

## 3. How huge pages help

x86-64 supports 2 MiB and 1 GiB pages. One TLB entry then covers the whole huge page.

| Page size | Second-level TLB coverage (est. entry counts) | Leaf tables per 1 TiB mapped | Reads per walk (4 levels) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4 KiB | 2048 × 4 KiB = 8 MiB | 2 GiB | 4 |
| 2 MiB | 2048 × 2 MiB = 4 GiB | 4 MiB | 3 |
| 1 GiB | 1024 × 1 GiB = 1 TiB | 8 KiB | 2 |

- **Larger coverage.** Each entry covers 512 times more memory with 2 MiB pages.
- **Shorter walk.** The walk stops one level earlier for 2 MiB pages. It stops two levels earlier for 1 GiB pages.
- **Smaller tables.** The leaf tables now fit in the CPU cache. So the remaining walk reads are fast.
- **Fewer page faults.** One fault maps 2 MiB instead of 4 KiB.

Linux offers two ways to get huge pages:

- **hugetlbfs.** The administrator reserves a fixed number of huge pages. The application requests them explicitly. A reserved page is guaranteed [Ref4].
- **THP.** The kernel uses a huge page when a free 2 MiB block exists. The application needs no change. Nothing is guaranteed [Ref5].

## 4. What can go wrong

**Reserved huge pages (hugetlbfs)**

- **Unusable memory.** Reserved pages are unavailable for any other use, even when idle [Ref4]. A reservation that is too large makes the remaining system run out of memory. On a shared server it also takes memory from the other users.
- **Late reservation fails.** After long uptime, free memory is split into small pieces. Then the kernel cannot form the huge pages. Reserve 1 GiB pages on the kernel command line at boot [Ref4].
- **Wrong NUMA node.** The reserved pages are divided between the nodes [Ref4]. A process bound to one node can find none there. It then gets an allocation error or SIGBUS (the bus error signal).
- **No swap.** The kernel cannot swap these pages out [Ref4].

**THP**

- **Pauses at page fault.** With `defrag=always`, the faulting thread waits during compaction [Ref5]. Compaction means the kernel moves pages to form a free 2 MiB block.
- **Higher memory use.** A write to one byte can allocate a full 2 MiB page. Sparse data structures then use much more memory [Ref5].
- **Fork.** Redis reports long pauses and high memory use after fork with THP on [Ref6]. Test this case if your service forks.
- **Background work.** khugepaged (the kernel thread that merges small pages) uses CPU time.
- **Results vary.** The number of free 2 MiB blocks decreases with uptime. So the same test can run at different speeds. Record the huge page coverage with every performance result.
- **Lower-risk setting.** The `madvise` mode limits THP to regions that the application marks [Ref5]. This confines most THP risks to that application.

**Both kinds**

- **Fewer TLB entries.** The first-level TLB has fewer entries for huge pages. A workload that accesses many distant regions then gains less. Est. counts for a recent Intel server core:
  - 4 KiB pages: 96 entries
  - 2 MiB pages: 32 entries
  - 1 GiB pages: 8 entries
- **Slow first write.** The kernel fills the whole page with zeros before first use. For a 1 GiB page this takes about 100 ms (est.).
- **Coarser NUMA placement.** A huge page is placed on one node as a whole. Threads on other sockets that share it need slower remote reads.
- **Virtual machines.** Guest and host must both use huge pages. Otherwise the TLB entry covers only the smaller size.

## 5. Numbers still missing for your server

Insufficient data: the exact TLB sizes, and the page walk cost of your workload. These commands measure them:

```bash
cpuid -1 | grep -i tlb            # TLB entry counts per page size
grep -i huge /proc/meminfo        # reserved pages and THP in use
cat /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/{enabled,defrag}   # THP mode
grep -E 'thp_fault_(alloc|fallback)|compact_stall' /proc/vmstat
perf stat -e cycles,dtlb_load_misses.walk_active,dtlb_store_misses.walk_active,itlb_misses.walk_active -- <command>
```

- Add the three `walk_active` counts and divide by `cycles`. The result is the approximate share of time in page walks.
- The `perf` event names are for Intel CPUs.
- Run the `perf` line with 4 KiB pages and with huge pages. The difference is the real gain for your workload.

## References

- [Ref2] Bhargava et al., "Accelerating Two-Dimensional Page Walks for Virtualized Systems", ASPLOS 2008.

- [Ref5] Linux kernel documentation, "Transparent Hugepage Support": https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/mm/transhuge.html
